messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: good news and bad news
parts:
Good news: scalability. I ran the "800 school" model (by just replicating the 8-schools data 100 times). I used Matt3's efficient parameterization. It took 8 seconds. That's amazingly fast. And it reached convergence.

Bad news: in one of the chains we got the following messages during adaptation:

********************************************************************************
Error in model.grad_log_prob:
Dynamic exception type: std::domain_error
std::exception::what: Error in function stan::prob::normal_log<N4stan5agrad3varE>(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter, mu,[0] is -inf:0, but must be finite!



********************************************************************************
Error in model.grad_log_prob:
Dynamic exception type: std::domain_error
std::exception::what: Error in function stan::prob::normal_log<N4stan5agrad3varE>(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter, mu,[0] is inf:0, but must be finite!




I don't know if this helps, but I will tell you that the model is not well behaved in this case. Recall that the data in the 8-schools are slightly under dispersed, i.e. the best estimate of tau from the data is actually negative. If you replicate 100 times, you basically get a dataset that's not consistent with the model. Given the constraints, tau really really wants to be zero. And when I re-fit using fake data simulated from the model, everything worked just fine.

That said, we _do_ sometimes fit models that don't fit the data, and we don't want Stan to be throwing errors. And I also can't figure out why mu, of all things, would be infinite.

Here's the model:

schools2_code <- '
data {
int<lower=0> J; // number of schools
real y[J]; // estimated treatment effects
real<lower=0> sigma[J]; // s.e. of effect estimates
}
parameters {
real mu;
real<lower=0> tau;
real eta[J];
}
transformed parameters {
real theta[J];
for (j in 1:J)
theta[j] <- mu + tau*eta[j];
}
model {
eta ~ normal(0,1);
y ~ normal (theta, sigma);
}
'


A
